description: We’re a multidisciplinary team interested in climate, health, and technology.
summary:
A home can fit a family’s budget and still expose them to climate-related health risks they have never considered. Climatch is a web application that helps families understand how the climate around their home may affect their health.

We developed a platform that transforms 25 years of NASA and NOAA data into understandable reports covering 10+ environmental risk factors, including heat, humidity, smoke, and air pollution. Users select a US location and provide household age groups and health conditions to receive a report highlighting relevant risks and practical ways to reduce exposure. Climatch prioritizes indicators relevant to the household and uses Mann–Kendall and Seasonal Kendall tests to identify statistically significant historical trends. Families considering a move can also compare 51 US cities against their own exposure limits.

Climatch addresses the challenge by turning complex Earth system data into evidence families can use. A home visit captures one moment; historical data reveals recurring exposure and long-term changes. By making these patterns accessible and personally relevant, Climatch helps homeowners address environmental concerns and homebuyers consider their family’s health alongside price and location.
details:
Families compare prices, schools, and commute times when choosing a home. Yet the conditions they will breathe, feel, and live with every day are harder to evaluate—especially when a child has asthma, an older parent needs care, or a family member has an existing health condition.

Climatch brings those health considerations into the conversation. It is a web application that helps families understand historical climate-related exposures around their home, identify which indicators deserve attention, and compare locations according to their household’s needs.

How it works

Users select a US address, city, or ZIP code and optionally enter household members’ age groups and health conditions. Climatch uses this information to prioritize relevant indicators in a personalized report. Personalization changes what receives attention, while keeping the underlying measurements and statistical findings consistent.

The report draws on 25 years of NASA and NOAA data, covering 10+ environmental factors such as heat, humidity, smoke, and air pollution. It explains how local conditions have changed, shows early and recent averages, and provides sourced information about practical ways to reduce exposure.

Mann–Kendall and Seasonal Kendall tests help distinguish statistically significant trends from year-to-year variation. Additional checks examine whether an unusual year drives the result, with corrections applied when multiple trends are tested. Families can explore the evidence behind each finding rather than rely on an unexplained score.

For those considering a move, Climatch compares 51 US cities against household-selected limits. It shows both exposure levels and historical changes, making trade-offs visible without declaring one city “best” for everyone.

Benefits and intended impact

For homeowners, the value is awareness that can lead to action. Climatch helps families recognize local exposures relevant to their health and explore measures to reduce them.

For homebuyers, the value is a more informed long-term decision. A property may meet a family’s financial and practical needs, while its surrounding climate deserves closer consideration. Climatch gives families evidence to include health-related concerns before committing.

For families and caregivers, the value is attention to different needs. A household is not one average person. By prioritizing indicators according to age and existing conditions, Climatch helps users focus on concerns relevant to the people they care for.

Our intended impact is to make health a more informed part of housing decisions. A home visit captures a moment; historical data reveals recurring exposure and lasting changes. Climatch makes that evidence understandable to people who would otherwise need to interpret complex scientific datasets themselves.

What makes Climatch creative?

Climatch connects the scale of Earth observation with the scale of family life. Its starting point is a personal question: “What does my family need to understand about living here?”

The innovation is in connecting three layers: historical environmental evidence, household-relevant interpretation, and practical location comparisons. Users can move from a plain-language finding to the underlying charts, statistical checks, and data limitations.

An interactive “detective” workflow also lets users investigate seasonal patterns, unusual events, and relationships between indicators. This helps families understand why a finding deserves attention and how much confidence to place in it.

Tools and development

We built the frontend using Next.js 16, React 19, Leaflet maps, and custom SVG charts on Figma. The backend uses Python and FastAPI, with a versioned API and an optional PostgreSQL cache.

Our data pipeline uses pandas, xarray, SciPy, and pymannkendall to transform NASA and NOAA observations into reports and maps. OpenStreetMap provides geographic context.

What we considered

Because Climatch connects environmental evidence with health concerns, we designed it around trust.

  • The platform describes historical exposure and prioritizes relevant indicators. It does not diagnose illness, predict an individual’s health outcome, or certify that a home is safe.
  • Household health information stays in the browser tab and is excluded from shared links, logs, and the database.
  • Reports show data sources, spatial resolution, available years, and limitations. Regional observations are not presented as measurements taken at a specific house.
  • Users choose their own comparison limits. The platform makes trade-offs visible rather than assigning a universal city ranking.
  • Mobile layouts, keyboard navigation, screen-reader descriptions, and cues beyond colour help more people use the evidence.
